speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when listening to various speeches that were made on this amendment I found it interesting to hear some hon. members agree with the amendment and then explain at great length why they must support the government motion. My position is simple in this regard. I have no hesitation whatever in fully supporting the amendment because anyone who is cognizant today of the conditions across this country, who knows the plight of the farmer, who knows the plight of the small businessman, who knows the plight of our many citizens who are on fixed income and facing rising prices due to inflation, could not help but be in sympathy with the terms of the amendment.
I listened with much interest to the address given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) this afternoon. He did a fine job of trying to explain fully not only the government's position but the various facts and figures that have been accumulated and put on the record. But, Mr. Speaker, it soon became evident, as is so often the case, that figures can tell both sides of a story.
Tonight, I would like to deal for a few minutes with the plight of our great agricultural industry and that of the small businessman. This afternoon, when explaining the slow increase in the rate of growth of farm income, the Minister of Finance said that this year we have had one of the greatest bumper crops in our history, and that the efficiency of the agricultural industry was increasing, thanks

to government action. No one will disagree with his statement that there has been a bumper crop of grain this year. It is fortunate that we have such a bumper crop and that we are able to find markets for it. But, Mr. Speaker, anyone inside this house or outside it would have the greatest difficulty in finding a single piece of legislation or action by the government that had anything to do with the increased efficiency of agriculture.
Over and over again the word "efficiency" creeps into discussions about the plight of agriculture. We are told that the farmer must increase his efficiency, and that in order to survive the family farm must increase its efficiency. We talk about the efficient large farm, the efficient family farm, the efficient co-operative farm but, Mr. Speaker, what do we mean?
Efficiency in agriculture could be looked upon with a great deal of envy by every other Canadian industry because the figures show that since world war II the average yearly efficiency rate of increase in farm production has been in the neighbourhood of 5.2 per cent, while the same figure for other Canadian industry has been 2 per cent. This is a remarkable record achieved by the farm industry.
I would like to give another set of figures to show how great the advance of agriculture in this direction has been. This average yearly increase in efficiency of 5.2 per cent has been created by 37 per cent fewer farmers, working with 32 per cent less labour, on 5 per cent less land.
Various government supporters, by illustration and debate, have sought to indicate that farmers have never had it so good. I wonder if they have stopped to consider what the facts actually are. Have they stopped to consider the reason that this great industry is losing farmers at the rate of 900 a month? When an economic survey of Canada was made about ten years ago it was estimated that between the years 1963 and 1970 the farm industry would lose 100,000 farmers. In actual fact, however, instead of losing 100,000 farmers by 1970 the industry, in a three year period from 1960, lost 100,000 farmers.
There is something radically wrong when we see farmers riding tractors on the roads, protesting that they are not receiving enough for their products. Surely, this must be a last resort for them to take. They must have taken it because they felt reason, argument and persuasion were of no avail. There is something wrong with the industry when, instead of being in a position to produce surpluses of all
November 22, 1966

food products for home consumption it cannot produce enough to meet our own demands.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
There is something wrong when each month we find that the very best cattle we have in this country are being exported and sold, not in the hundreds but in the thousands. There is something drastically wrong when we find that many of the fruits and vegetables which previously were so common in this country are either in short supply or are not grown. The reason is that those who have produced these products, sometimes for three generations, find it no longer is economically feasible to do so. There is something wrong when in this nation of 20 million people, where we have for so long been producers of surplus agricultural supplies, we now import an estimated $14 billion to $2 billion worth of food and food products annually.
"Never had it so good"; well, Mr. Speaker, my considered opinion is that the fruit and vegetable industry in Canada has never been in a more precarious position than it is at the present time. I do not think so many of our efficient and successful farmers, and so many of our corporate farms, should be on the edge of bankruptcy as there are today. Yet, the government suggests that we never have had it so good.
The farmers of this country and the small business men are looking to this government for leadership. They are looking for policies. It is all right to say an entire program is being introduced for the war on poverty. Does one have to be absolutely destitute, does one have to be on bended knee with arms out for alms before this government will take any action? These citizens of Canada want leadership, and they want a policy while they still have businesses in which they can incorporate this policy to earn a livelihood for themselves and their families. "Never had it so good"-well, when you see businesses, small construction companies, small lumber dealers, the corner grocery store, the dry goods shops, automobile agencies and all the small businesses in town after town across the country closing their doors because they find it is not economically sound to operate, then something is drastically wrong.
To be absolutely fair, all of these people cannot and will not be helped by any government policy. There certainly are changing circumstances. There are changing market trends; there are changing buying patterns; there are changing products and different territories. All of these things come into this
Increased Cost of Living problem and are causing small businesses to face grave hardships. However, I think one of the greatest threats facing businesses and farmers today is the fact that under this government they never are certain of their credit rating. During the time this government has been in office, there has been either a feast or a famine; there has appeared to be either no limit on the credit or no credit at all.
As one who has been and is associated with farmers, I took very violent exception to the fact that this government was doubling the amount of money farmers could obtain under the farm improvement loan fund and the farm credit corporation. I was afraid of the outcome. Events have proven that we on this side of the house who took that stand were correct, because all this money which some two years ago was placed in the hands of young farmers and established farmers did not help these men. All these millions of dollars which were put into the hands of these farmers did nothing but inflate the value of farm land and bring about a drastic increase in the price of farm machinery. This has made it much more difficult for a young farmer or an established farmer to operate a farm. It did not settle anything; it did not solve anything. There has been absolutely no progress toward a solution.
When one considers that this government has been in office since 1963, it would seem that they certainly must have had time to initiate and put into effect some policies which would help this great industry of agriculture, the small businessmen and which would do something for these small country towns and villages which are dying. One would have thought that they would have implemented some of the promises they have made in this regard.
I do not intend to go step by step through the record of the Conservative government when it was in office; nor do I intend to go step by step through the record of this government since it has been in office. I do not think the farmers and small businessmen are interested in the records. They are interested in knowing what the plans are for progress in the future. They want to know whether or not the government knows where agriculture is going; they want to know whether the government has any idea at all what the future is for small businesses; they want to know whether there is a concerted plan of action or whether the government is going along day by day and, as a matter of political expediency, deal with the problem which is creating the greatest havoc at this particular time.

November 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living [DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, it is the considered opinion of farm leaders and businessmen's associations across this country that in order to survive in this competitive world we face today we can no longer go by the rule of thumb but have to accept every bit of advice, knowledge and recommendation which is available from the various scientists, technicians and economists who are in a position to judge where we are now and where we should go in the future. This is the reason I have nothing but the greatest admiration for the provincial ministers of agriculture and provincial departments of trade and commerce which have initiated what this government should have initiated three years ago. I refer to the conferences at which they bring in the leaders of all groups to find out what is necessary for agriculture and where agriculture should go. How can men, whose every waking hour is directed toward the production of quantity and quality produce here in Canada, take the necessary time from their busy lives to investigate future market trends. How can they investigate the needs of all these new and developing countries, the new processes whereby raw products can be used to form new products acceptable to other parts of the world? How can they investigate the drifting and changing patterns of buyers both abroad and at home, the quantities of food, that will be needed for the home market in the next 20 years? Will our production exceed the domestic and export demand? If our production increases at the present rate, will it become greater than we will need? In other words, Mr. Speaker, where do we go from here?
I fail to see how any sound businessman in agriculture today can formulate any production plans for the future unless he has available some real source of information. Where is it more natural for him to turn than the federal government, with all its vast departments and resources which are capable of foretelling and forecasting markets and providing him with the necessary information? If this government does not initiate such programs; if it does not know where agriculture is going, if it does not care for long range programs, then its members have no right to say to the farmers and small businessmen of this nation: You have never had it so good.
There is a standing committee of this house dealing with consumer credit and the high cost of food products. I believe that every man on that committee is putting every bit of effort possible into finding a solution and

finding out just where we are going. But this committee was initiated by the housewives across the nation who felt that the price of food was too high and decided to do something about it. It was not initiated by the government. There was a cry of distress that came from the people. Is it not strange that, on one hand, we have this cry of distress from the housewives of our nation over the tremendously high prices they are constantly being asked to pay for foodstuffs and, on the other hand, we have a mass migration of farmers off the farms? We have tractor parades protesting the low prices which the farmer receives for his products.
When you have these two great factions mounting protests and directing them to the government in Ottawa, is it not time that the government enunciated a policy in this respect? I am one of those who believes that the time has come, and is perhaps long overdue, when the Department of Agriculture should concern itself not only with the production of food for Canada and for export but should maintain standards of quality in the production of food for our people. I favour a step taken by the department of agriculture of Ontario in this respect. They felt that the department should be responsible for all the different stages of food production, from the harvesting of the raw product until it falls into the hands of the consumer. I believe this is a field into which the Department of Agriculture could move and try, by careful analysis and deliberation, to bring some sort of regulation out of the chaos in which we find ourselves today.
There is certainly something wrong when the price of the finished product to the consumer can be many, many times the price paid to the farmer. I am not one who believes that there is any particular culprit in this situation. I cannot believe that in every instance there is excess profit-taking. It may be that our methods of marketing do not lend themselves to the most economic way of placing food in the hands of the consumer. It may be that there are services that are either not as efficient as they might be, or there is a duplication of services. This matter should be investigated.
But surely, the time has come when all the segments of this country that are crying out for relief should have their supplications to the government answered. As I said before, it is not sufficient to cite facts and figures in an economic report. It is not enough to say that according to the records the gross production of the farms of this nation is on the increase,
November 22, 1966

when the farm population is dropping to the drastically low figure to which it has dropped. This fact was corroborated by the Minister of Finance this afternoon when he stated that at one time there were over one million families in this great nation of ours engaged primarily in the production of food, and today there are about half this number. Something is radically wrong if this is the situation.
The only place to which we can go for redress is the federal government. The provincial governments are doing everything they can, but their scope is limited. They have to deal with specific problems in a specific, designated area. Very often measures designed at the federal level to help one area work to the detriment of farmers in another area.
I want to give this government credit; it is endeavouring to set up various commissions which it feels will settle some of the problems which face our agricultural industry today. The government has set up the dairy commission and the feed grain commission. These are new bodies and they will be on trial. I hope they can solve the problems they were designed to solve. But it seems to me we are delaying and procrastinating to such a degree that the farm industry may face economic ruin before concrete steps are taken on a large enough scale to provide the relief that is necessary.
There is one other point with which I should like to deal, and I am sure it is one with which many members of this house are directly concerned. I speak of the trade negotiations going on in Geneva at the present time under GATT, where they are considering an eradication or reduction of tariffs on goods entering this country.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
I think one of the greatest sources of uneasiness, especially among farmers engaged in the production of fruit and vegetables, is their worry that they will have to face once again drastically reduced tariffs on their particular products in exchange for favourable consideration of industrial products or other services. They fear a situation in which their businesses might absolutely collapse over night. I was very young when the last collapse occurred, but I shall never forget walking through farm after farm and seeing acre after acre of fruits and vegetables rotting on the ground. The newspapers were full of advertisements by the farmers begging people to come and pick the crops for nothing. They wrote "you can have it if you come and get
Increased Cost of Living it". The price of those crops was so low that the town population would not bother to go to the farms and get them; they asked the farmers to deliver them. We do not want to see this happen again. We do not ever want to see the green belt industry which was built up in Ontario collapse as a result of negotiations with which these farmers and small businessmen had very little to do.
These men, for the most part, have not the faintest idea who the Canadian negotiators are who are dealing with the very lifeblood of their industry. They have no idea of the proposed reductions in their particular crops which the Canadian government is prepared to accept. All they know is that the basis of this entire treaty was a proposal by the United States government for an across the board 50 per cent reduction in the tariff rates in many of the commodities that are grown in Ontario. This 50 per cent reduction in tariffs would mean the absolute ruin of families which, in many instances, have invested $500,000 in their farms and businesses. When these industries have to survive in an economic climate in which they have no idea what will happen in the next 12 months, do you not think they deserve an answer to some of these questions? Is it not time that the government enunciated a policy for agriculture and small industries? It is not sufficient for the government to say: "We have initiated plans for a war on poverty. You never had it so good. The national productivity of this country is increasing at a more rapid rate than ever before."
This may be true in the cities, but it is not true on the farms. It is not true when many small business men have to move out of establishments which have been operating sometimes for as long as 20 years. There is something radically wrong when these people are forced out of business. When this happens, at least they have the right to know what government policy forced them out.
This is why, when we have an amendment before us which states that the government has failed to introduce policies over a three year period which would indicate that the people of Canada can move forward, I fail to see how anybody could decline to support such an amendment. I have absolutely no patience for any representative of the people who understands what the citizens of Canada are going through and then says: "I cannot support such an amendment." The people of Canada will no longer tolerate a party which

November 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living straddles the fence on economic issues. Indeed, it grieves me to walk down the streets of some of the towns which I represent and see another empty store.
There is something wrong when, as a result of this government's changed policies, a construction man who had a crew of 12 men engaged in the business of painting houses finds that because of the numerous obligations with which he was forced to comply, the reports which he had to fill out, and because of a scarcity of money, he cannot pay for the necessary accoutrements his business requires. To see such a man tell his employees they have to seek work elsewhere, and to see him become an employee himself after years of being an employer is a sad state of affairs.
We often hear that agriculture no longer represents a political force in the country today, and will no longer exert the same influence on politicians which it did formerly. In the province of Ontario, which is probably more industrialized than any other province in Canada and which contains approximately 40 per cent of our population, 30 per cent of the labour force is directly engaged in agriculture or in allied industries. Let no one say that today agriculture no longer represents a political force in the world.
May I say in conclusion that I have not the least hesitation in supporting this amendment which points out to the country as a whole that this government has failed in its obligation to the Canadian people to bring forth policies which will aid the ordinary Canadian to provide a living for himself and his family. It is not sufficient to point to social legislation and to say: "We will take care of you when you are old; you will get a government grant when you are sick; if you are injured, we will help you". The people of Canada want an economic climate which will enable them to make an honest living. They want an honest return for an honest day's work in the production of goods. They are entitled to this. I cannot support a government which does not provide the people of Canada with this opportunity.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Bas-ford) is not in his seat, because I wanted to thank him for the kind references he made yesterday and also to tell him in return that I think he makes an excellent co-chairman of the consumer prices committee. However, I cannot follow him when he indicates

that this motion represents a lack of confidence in what the committee is trying to achieve. I have every confidence in what the consumer prices committee is trying to do, but this does not mean that I have every confidence in our present system of distributing goods and services in Canada. Indeed, the consumer prices committee, beyond the shadow of a doubt, has served only to confirm my solid conviction that our method of distributing goods and services to the consumers of Canada leaves a great deal to be desired.
For one thing, our system of getting goods and services to the consumers at the present time is riddled with abuses of all sorts. I am not going to take the time tonight to detail these abuses, but anyone who has attended two or three sessions of the committee will have become conscious of the way the consumer is being conned, gulled and deceived and is taken for a ride at every turn. Also, from the standpoint of the consumer our present system of distributing goods and services is wasteful, inefficient, unjust and in many respects out of date.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the committee is doing a good job in bringing this fact to light. From my own observations may I say I do not think there will be anything left to be revealed if the committee has its way. However, in this regard I cannot help but remember the price spreads commission which reported in 1934 and the more recent royal commission, the Stewart commission, which reported less than ten years ago. What happened to the results of the very heavy work of the members of those commissions? Their reports were pigeonholed and they have been gathering dust ever since. My only fear is that when this committee finishes its work and completes its very onerous task its report too may join the others in gathering dust in a pigeonhole.
This is where the government comes in, Mr. Speaker. If it is sincere in setting up this committee to investigate rising prices in Canada and cares for the interests of the consumers, the government will see to it that the report of the committee does not suffer the same fate but will be prepared to deal with it. But I fear, that the government has not yet shown that it understands the significance of what is being revealed by the consumer prices committee or, if it does understand the significance of these revelations, that it is not prepared to give the leadership necessary to bring about the required changes.
November 22, 1966	COMMONS
Before I turn to the motion specifically there is one other matter to which I should like to add a bit of information. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard referred yesterday to the fact that the Swedish equivalent of John Deutsch, if you want to call him that, Professor Kragh, appeared before the committee. The hon. member and others have subsequently said that Professor Kragh referred to Canada's until very lately relatively steady price level and to the fact that Canada's price level was so much less than that in other countries. Indeed, these hon. members produced figures to show that in a survey of the cost of living in 27 countries during the period 1958 to May, 1966 Canada had the second lowest increase in prices, namely, 15 per cent. Sweden, with an increase of 33 per cent, was among the highest.
The moral they drew from this, Mr. Speaker, was that we in Canada should not be making complaints about rising price levels because prices in Canada have risen only 15 per cent whereas in Sweden they have gone up 33 per cent. But the part of the story given by Dr. Kragh that these hon. members left out was this. Under questioning Dr. Kragh said that pensions and allowances in Sweden were geared, and I quote his words, "100 per cent to the cost of living in that country". In other words, Swedish old age pensioners, veterans and others who receive social allowances of various kinds do not need to worry when the cost of living goes up because their pensions and allowances are geared to the rising cost of living. When price levels rise these pensions and allowances rise automatically. This means that the people of Sweden know that rising prices do not mean in turn lower living standards for the lower income groups in the country. I wanted to point that out because I think it is tremendously important.
It was suggested, Mr. Speaker, that Dr. Kragh might be envious of our prices record in Canada. Dr. Kragh might find some things to be envious about, but I am sure that he would not be envious of our record of price rises, particularly if he were to reflect upon what they have done to the poorer groups of the country, our old age pensioners and others.
I now come to the specific amendment we are debating. It has been read a number of times so I do not need to read it again. I feel it is exceedingly significant that at the beginning of the debate the government seemed disposed to brush the motion aside as of little consequence. Indeed, it seemed to be considered far out, crackpot, and all the usual things
Increased Cost of Living said by way of objection were trotted out. However, as the debate has proceeded I have noticed much more of a disposition on the part of hon. members to reflect on what the amendment means and upon the conditions which brought it into being. There has been a tremendous change in atmosphere and the amendment has been taken very seriously.
I will not refer to the oratory of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin). As a matter of fact, I think this thing hit him so suddenly that he was unable to adjust to it. His first reaction was one of blind indignation. He rather reminded me of the story I heard about the young lawyer who was very nervously going over his brief, marking places with instructions to himself for the awful moment when he would be addressing the jury. He marked certain instructions like "Go slow", "Pause here", "A little greater emphasis", and so on. Finally he marked one spot in this way: "Case here very weak, shout like hell". I felt that this was a little like what the hon. member for St. John's West was doing, just shouting in order to obscure the fact that this question should be taken very seriously indeed.
Other members, Mr. Speaker, have taken this amendment as symptomatic of a very serious condition indeed. I was interested in the appeal made by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) that in face of the situation now confronting us we should consider all ideas, no matter whether or not they came from the newer groups in the house. If they were ideas which gave some promise for dealing with the situation and tackling the problem in a new way, they should be considered.
The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) spoke in the debate and I was very pleased to see his conversion to the idea of a prices review board. He voted against such a board on March 22, but evidently the logic of the events which have taken place has convinced him, as it also convinced the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), that a prices review board is a very necessary part of the machinery that the government should be using today. I congratulate these hon. members for not hesitating to change their minds when they saw it was a good thing to do so.
I feel that the ultimate tribute to the seriousness with which this amendment is taken was to have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) enter the debate. He saw fit to lock horns with the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). I am not going to

November 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living get into this battle of figures because I have heard figures used in different ways to prove so many things that I do not intend to muddy the water still more. But I believe that the minister knew only too well the seriousness of this amendment when he referred to the fact that one of the grave problems confronting us today is the lopsidedness of income distribution in Canada.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
The Minister of Finance knows that no amount of playing with figures will disguise what is revealed in government figures and submissions, that a quarter of our population is living either in poverty or in various degrees of destitution under the poverty line. You cannot get that out of the way by running down this party's amendment to deal with incomes. Neither can you ignore the facts presented by the hon. member for Kent Ont. (Mr. Danforth) when he showed what has been happening to the farmers. In Canada 30 per cent of the farmers are producing 70 per cent of farm products, and the government has to use policies to get marginal farmers off the land to bolster our agriculture. Old farmers have to be retrained or if they cannot be retrained they must be given a subsistence allowance for the rest of their days. This is new in Canada, and you cannot get away from what is happening by shouting that the amendment is far out and beside the point.
Neither can you ignore the strikes we are having in this country. Strikes do not occur for fun or for the heck of it. Through strikes workers attempt to redress a balance and try to get their share of productivity, because the workers know that productivity in this country has been going up. Now the workers are beginning to catch up, but there is no denying that the situation has been lopsided, it is lopsided income distribution which will continue causing strikes.
The Minister of Finance pointed to certain things which have been done by way of the Canada Assistance Plan and handouts of various kinds. That does not blur for a moment the clarity of the picture, because in Canada incomes are lopsided and are becoming more lopsided as the cost of living rises. This is the picture you cannot get away from and this is the picture to which we draw attention in our amendment. All session we have been asking, as have the Canadian people, what the government intends to do about the rising cost of living. Every time we have asked we have been told, "Wait until the Economic Council brings in its report before the end of the year;

then we shall be able to answer your questions." Well, we have been reading the report and some of us have done some work on it, but we are not reassured that the central problems facing us will be solved.
I will not go into anything deeply tonight but one can read in the press-I have here the Globe and Mail-that the Economic Council says that guidelines will not work in Canada. On the other side of the page I see a heading, "Delay Major Policy Changes, Economic Council says". In other words, the suggestions made will not work and this is no time to make major policy changes. In the actual report the Economic Council points out that there is nothing new, there is no magical formula, just the old trusted and tried remedies to be tried and tried again. I say to the government that it is the opinion of this group and other members of the house that these tried and trusted remedies which have brought us to this mess will not get us out of it. The suggestions in the report are in the category of thinking you can cure yourself with the hair of the dog that bit you.
We do not believe that playing along with the same methods of a bit here and there, the Canada Assistance Plan today and medicare put off once again till tomorrow, certain relief provisions to parts of our population and the proposal to raise the old age pension but undercut the raise by a means test, which will set us back to before 1951, will work. These things and this way of carrying on will not solve our problems.
Somebody has suggested that we ought to have what is known as an incomes policy. I do not know what we shall do about an incomes policy but I do know that on page 160 of the third annual review of the Economic Council of Canada we see that they say:
-the policy would apply to both prices and wages: a more one-sided approach would be a political and economic non-starter.
In the rest of the paragraph there is not a single word about profits. They talk about prices and wages but there is not a word about profits. The time has come for the government to realize that productivity, profits, prices, wages, salaries and income, that is, pensions and allowances and income of all kinds, are inseparably tied together in one package. You cannot deal with one of these things satisfactorily without dealing with the whole package. Productivity, profits, prices, wages and salaries, and incomes such as pensions and allowances are tied together inseparably and must be treated together and
November 22, 1966

brought together into some kind of meaningful relation. Otherwise we shall have no way or redressing the lopsided income picture which this government's policies have created. Doing what I suggest is the only way by which there can be an adequate and suitable division of the production of our industrialized country.
The Minister of Finance said he had no objection to a fair distribution of the industrial products of this country. I say that there is only one way we can have fair distribution, and that is by the government's giving leadership in looking at those factors mentioned today and yesterday. The government must examine the relation among productivity and profits, prices, wages and salaries, pensions and allowances. Until the government gives leadership in examining this whole picture we shall not get the sort of thing we have referred to in the amendment. Hon. members may remember that it refers to an equitable distribution of rising productivity and national income among all groups in Canada, particularly in view of the rising cost of living.
Let me point out that introducing measures for housing, trade or anything else will not do the job because if you deal with only one of the factors in the picture at a time one part of the population will be in competition with the other and the result will not be good. Taking these things piecemeal may have been all right in more simple times but today we have automation and already in our economy we have great competition. It adds up to chaos and injustice, and disorders of one sort or another such as strikes, farm marches and housewives' demonstrations will continue to plague us unless something is done. The Economic Council says that certain things can be done.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
Today Sweden has reached a stage of maturity-it has taken a long time-where representatives of the manufacturers' association for the whole country and representatives of labour for the whole country sit down together to plan the bargaining for the year for all the country's industries. They plan within a fairly narrow range and they plan with the productivity of the country foremost in their minds. Both parties know they cannot get all they want and they sit down to bargain keeping the productivity of the country in mind. Manufacturers and trade unions have to bargain back and forth in order to work these
Increased Cost of Living things out, but the Economic Council has indicated that this policy will not work in Canada at this time in our present stage of immaturity and lagging development. This is what we must work toward. There is validity in what the Economic Council has suggested but I feel that the government is not trying to find methods which will engender development and solutions to the difficulties that lie ahead. Instead the government is using these difficulties as a reason for not working toward a policy of income balance with productivity with a resultant equality of distribution in all sectors.
The Economic Council is using the constitutional rights established by the B.N.A. Act as the reason for not providing more social equality in Canada, just as the government in the 1920's used them in an attempt to avoid providing old age pensions. That government successfully hid behind that act until it realized that people in this country did not intend to put up with any more of this nonsense.
When we have experienced enough strikes, housewives' marches and farm tractor slowdowns perhaps this government or its successor will settle down and find ways and means of providing the necessary income redistribution programs in spite of our constitution. The government has suggested that the provinces will not stand any interference in this regard but I was impressed by what Laurier La-Pierre said the other day to a group of teachers in the province of Quebec, and I quote from the Montreal Star of November 19, 1966:
Too long, also, have we been presented with a false picture of the priority of provincial needs based on a concept of superior and inferior levels of government, and of the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in certain areas.
Farther on the article states:
Professor LaPierre suggested that Quebec did not have much catching up to do with the rest of Canada "because there's nothing much to catch up to". He struck out at what he called the "era of oratorical nationalism. It doesn't really matter what you say, as long as you yell like hell about it." And the situation, he added, was not peculiar to Quebec, but "to all of Canada."
The Canadian people are waiting for this government to give leadership in solving the difficulties which stand in the way of obtaining a proper distribution of income in this country. These difficulties are regional, constitutional and organizational. Perhaps they are the result of immaturity among various sectors of this country. It is too bad that the Economic Council considers these problems cannot be solved at this time because this

November 22, I960
Increased Cost of Living government will have to solve them soon or we will have to get a government that will. The people are becoming thoroughly sick and tired of being fobbed off by the adoption of inefficient security legislation only when they yell hard enough and long enough. The people are seeking a fair and equitable relationship between prices and income.
Let me say quite seriously that the kind of legislation referred to in the amendment proposed by this party is the kind of legislation we will hear about increasingly in this day and age. This is not a hangover from the old days when social justice was desirable. Social justice has now become imperative because of our rapidly changing economy. The government can no longer get by with promises or the provision of a modicum of assistance. The government must provide leadership in obtaining an equitable distribution of income. Canada is a growing country and the people expect our income distribution programs to grow at the same pace.

I was pleased this afternoon to note that the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) participated in this debate. His speeches are always accurate, objective and reflect his sincere regard for the plight of senior citizens in Canada. I was delighted to note that he was able to partake in this debate because it is an indication he has regained his health. All of us, I am sure, shared in the grief of the Tory party when that hon. member was stricken with a heart attack not too long ago. We are pleased that he is back in the house and will welcome again his contributions to our debates.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
I listened this afternoon to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) and I will refer to him from now on

as the hon. member because such a picturesque and beautiful constituency name should not be distorted by my inability to pronounce it correctly. I was rather surprised and a little bit upset when the hon. member made reference to a link between the Mafia and the Liberal party. I was disappointed when he made that reference and in the next sentence referred to the Munsinger case and the Tory party. I was disappointed that any member of the New Democratic Party would introduce this into the debate because I had hoped it was a closed chapter in the House of Commons. I was also surprised because obviously it is a deviation from their plan to portray at all times to the Canadian people the rather sanctimonious attitude that they are above this type of mudslinging. It became obvious to me that the hon. member, irked because of the aggressive but correct parliamentary tactics of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin), thought this was one way to retaliate. I only hope the hon. member now realizes he has shown the people of Canada that the members of the N.D.P. are human also.
The amendment before the house is very cleverly designed-

In case hon. members think that the socialists do not know what they are doing so far as politics is concerned, I think it only fair to point out that a recent Gallup poll has shown that the fortunes of war of that party, at least temporarily, are on an equal basis with those of the Tory party in Canada. I do not think they will remain that way because, while none of us relish the problems that the Tory party may be having at the moment, the one fundamental difference between the two major parties in this country and the New Democratic Party is that the two major parties stand for the free enterprise system while the N.D.P., despite all its propaganda at its periodic conventions, has never really strayed too far from the Regina manifesto of the 1930's.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway went on to say that we must control prices, that we must control wages and, of course, that we must deny profits. She said that the Economic Council had never mentioned profits in its report and, of course, profits is a

November 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living dirty word in the socialist system. At least the hon. member is honest in that respect.
The success that the N.D.P. has had with 26 per cent of the Canadian electorate has been due to its ability to confuse the electorate and hide the fact that basically it stands for socialism while the two major parties in this house stand for the free enterprise system. That would not be too bad if at least hon. members of that party modified or refined their philosophy. But there was a noticeable similarity in the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) and the hon. member for V ancouver-Kingsway.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands put all the blame for Canadian economic problems on corporations. He said that big corporations in some mysterious fashion were responsible for all our problems. Instead of members of the socialist party standing up here whining and crying about the economic problems of Canada, I contend that at least they should be objective and quote those sections of the report of the Economic Council which state quite emphatically that all countries in the western world that have a free enterprise system are in the midst of an economic boom.
It is true that there are Canadians who cannot share in the boom, but the N.D.P. skilfully creates the impression that it and it alone is interested in these people. This is unfair to the other parties in the House of Commons. Members of the N.D.P. have tried to discredit the benefits of the Canada Assistance Plan, but I can tell them that people in my riding, such as widows at the age of 38 left with three children under four years of age, are very thankful for the Canada Assistance Plan. A father who is left with four children and who is able to get financial assistance to hire a housekeeper also knows the benefit of that plan, which is the first of its type we have ever had in Canada. I suspect that the hon. member spoke without thinking and on reflection will on another occasion apologize for her remarks about that particular piece of welfare legislation.
It is time that the N.D.P., through the medium of parliament, told the Canadian people what it stands for. If the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has such a dim view of large corporations and takes pleasure from the fact that he went out to lunch with big money men as if they were something to be sneezed at, then let him say so. Let his party say in its pamphlets and
[Mr. Mackasey.l
speeches by Laurier LaPierre and others, that once elected they will destroy corporations as they exist today. [DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
Look at the problems that this party left behind it. Why do they constantly refer to Sweden, Denmark and England? Why do they not tell us about the sorry mess they made in Saskatchewan? Why do they not tell us about the untapped mineral wealth that lies beneath the ground in the form of potash and which lay dormant during the 15 or 20 years of the socialist regime? The reason is that no private enterprise would risk the capital to exploit those projects.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? Would he agree that perhaps the centralizing tendencies put into effect when Hon. C. D. Howe was minister of trade and commerce had a great deal to do with the number of people who left the province of Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
I do not know what the hon. member is getting at. He is talking about the centralizing policies of Mr. C.D. Howe which I think got out of hand although possibly they were policies which were necessary during the war years. It is interesting to note, however, that the hon. member who just spoke for the socialists mentioned a few moments ago that according to the Economic Council many of the steps she has advocated such as price control, wage control and profit control are unconstitutional because of the terms of the B.N.A. Act. Yet she stands up and says in effect, "To hell with the B.N.A. Act. There must be some way around it; we got around it when pensions were introduced." But at the same time New Democratic Party spokesmen in the province of Quebec who are going back and forth trying to induce English speaking and French speaking Quebeckers to endorse their policies are exemplifying themselves as the greatest advocates of provincial rights ever discovered in this country.
In this day of modern communications the time has come when representatives of the New Democratic Party cannot get up in the House of Commons and say in one breath, "To hell with the B.N.A. Act, we do not recognize provincial rights under the B.N.A. Act", and the next day make a speech at McGill University, the University of Montreal or at the university in Trois-Rivieres saying, "We stand for provincial rights". You cannot have the best of two worlds. You might have been able to do it 50 years ago when we did not have the sophistication we have now in the field of communications. You cannot do so any more. You have to be consistent in what you say. So I simply think that perhaps the New Democratic Party should realize that expressing one philosophy in the House of Commons and another on the hustings in the province of Quebec is going to catch up to them sooner or later. People will compare notes and ask how a party can on the one hand favour something which is a complete violation of provincial
Increased Cost of Living rights and then on the other hand stand up before the voters of Quebec and say, "You must vote for us because we are the one party which respects provincial rights". You cannot advocate both.
The hon. member who referred to Mr. C. D. Howe knows as well as I do that many of the problems which we are suffering from today have arisen from the kind of attitude which existed during the war years when we could not be quite so fussy about provincial rights because of the war effort. But those days have gone by. If we are to have the peace and prosperity in this country which everyone wants, the federal government will have to learn to respect the rights of the provincial governments, whether that government happens to be Quebec, British Columbia, Saskatchewan or Manitoba. There are certain things according to the B.N.A. Act which are sacred, such things as education for example, and some areas about which the hon. member said, "Well, to hell with them, let us introduce price control". You cannot do this in Canada. You could do it in Sweden. The N.D.P. could have done many of these things in Saskatchewan because they were the provincial government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
I do not wish to get into a battle with the hon. lady. She did mention the B.N.A. Act. She did admit that the Economic

November 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living Council report stated that such controls were unconstitutional and illegal, but then she went on to say that there must be some way in which we can circumvent the constitution as was done in 1926. That is what she is saying. The trouble with the N.D.P. is that the major parties in the House of Commons are supposed to sit here day after day and listen to the N.D.P. tell us what is wrong with our two parties. They lecture us rather than enter into the debate. Somehow they have created the illusion in Canada that the happy little band of warriors in the New Democratic Party have some God-given right to lecture others because they know what it is that is bothering Canada. They lecture us about our responsibilities to the senior citizens, creating the impression that they and they alone are concerned about the senior citizens. Then the hon. lady stands up and says there is nothing good about the Canada Assistance Plan. If the hon. lady thought so, she should at least have stood up on second reading and said so. During the 1930's in the depression days the people did not have an opportunity to put away money to look after their retirement. We should not regard our social welfare measures as constituting handouts.
What we are debating here is the amendment and this is the reason my remarks are directed to the New Democratic Party. The amendment reads:
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
-since the income of wage and salary earners has remained approximately the same and farm income has fallen as a proportion of the total national income over a period of years, this house regrets the failure of the government to introduce policies-
If the leader of the New Democratic Party were honest he would at least have said in his amendment "regrets the failure of the policies introduced by the government". To create the impression that no policies have been introduced by the government is unfair. The amendment goes on to say:
-designed to produce an equitable distribution of ...national income among all groups in Canada-
I am sure hon. members would agree that social welfare measures fall into that pattern. What do social welfare measures do? The philosophy behind family allowances was to put in the hands of particular people in Canada, presumably the mothers or the parents, money to spend. This is distribution of wealth. This is what social welfare measures do. This is why I do not share the fear of many people that if we introduce too many social welfare measures in Canada we shall be
[Mr. Mackasey.l
on the road to bankruptcy or will be creating debts which we cannot meet. The idealistic solution to depression is to put as much money as we can into the hands of the people, provided that they will go out and spend it and not hoard it under the mattress. So social welfare measures certainly should not be belittled as having an adverse effect on our distribution of wealth.
We should be proud of our private enterprise system which has given us one of the highest standards of living in the world. This system has been able to generate the money necessary for the two major parties which have formed the government in this country to live up to their moral commitments to our senior citizens. When we pass the legislation increasing the old age pension, which will be fairly soon, and now that the principle of the medicare program has been adopted, the social welfare measures enjoyed by Canadian citizens will be second to none in the free world.
Last summer I spent the better part of a month with the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) in a country behind the Iron Curtain. There you have all the ingredients necessary for the implementation of socialistic philosophy. There the workers have nothing to worry about. Food is supplied in huge quantities, even if there is a great deal of potatoes and very little meat. Rent is paid and there is free hospitalization. Everything is supplied. But what is denied these people? They are denied the incentive, the drive that the private enterprise system generates in this country, the United States and the free world.
How many people behind the Iron Curtain, who are denied the right to live under the private enterprise system with all the imperfections we have been hearing about today, would not come here if they had an opportunity? I felt sick in Poland and got to know a doctor very well. She was a young lady of 28.

able to take in the occasional patient by the back door, they calculate that in three years time they will be able to afford a scooter and in five years time they will be able to afford a little automobile. These are professional people.
I asked the minister of labour of Poland when they last had a strike in that country. We were talking about the large number of strikes other countries had been experiencing. She said to me-I say "she" because the minister of labour of Poland happens to be a lady and is also president of the textile unions -quite gravely that the last time they had a strike in Poland was 1956. I am not the greatest historian in the world but I remember what happened in Poland and Hungary in 1956. If you call that a strike, I say it is an understatement. So I would not exchange one ounce of our private enterprise system, with all its imperfections, for the whole of socialism.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
I should like to say something else about the amendment. It appeals to the farmers of this country. The New Democratic Party had an opportunity to do something for the farmers of this country. They dropped them in 1960. They changed their name from the C.C.F. to the N.D.P. and in effect said to the farmers: Here is the end of the merry-go-round, fellows. We had better infiltrate the labour movement because it is obvious that as long as we stick with the farmer we will not have an opportunity of forming the government of this country.
At least the Tory and Liberal parties stand for a system that respects the dignity of man and includes a degree of incentive. This incentive is not part of the socialist philosophy. We share with the New Democratic Party concern for the senior citizens and the unfortunates of this country. We share their concern for the plight of those farmers who live in uneconomic regions. But are we really being fair to the farmer by keeping him on land that cannot possibly be profitable to operate? How many of the western farmers in the house have told me, including the hon. member who was with me in Poland when speaking to a group of farmers in that country, that they do not want anything to do with the co-operative movement? The farms out west are profitable because they are now efficient. The farmers have learned to operate huge pieces of machinery which have made their operations more efficient. This has made it possible for 23033-646
Increased Cost of Living us to sell our wheat in markets across the world; we have found that we are able to reap and market it economically.
If there are farmers in this country whose plot of land is too small, who live too far from markets, who find it impossible to live on the income obtained from their farms, we are not doing them any favour by giving them handouts. Neither is any member of this House of Commons doing them any favour by rising and saying that the government is unfair to the farmers because their income is so low. There are many farms that are uneconomic today. This was the whole basis of the principles of ARDA, which the Conservative party introduced and we enlarged. This amendment tries to tell the people of Canada that we have introduced no measures to share the wealth. The leader of the New Democratic Party has been accused of many things, but he is not naive. He knows, as all of us know, the efforts that have been made in this house since 1962 by our government and, I presume, by the previous government before 1962 to create the Utopian type of living whereby everybody is without want and disease. We are getting closer to that ideal.
No mention was made by the hon. lady or others of that party about the effects of the Canada Pension Plan which in a few years will do a great deal to alleviate the worry, concern and anxiety of our senior citizens. We are now trying to look after those people caught in the time gap until the Canada Pension Plan reaches full maturity. For the New Democratic Party members to rise sanctimoniously and say, "Put us in office, we will correct everything", is nonsense. I spent half an hour listening to the hon. lady because I consider her to be one of the most intelligent members of that party and certainly the best looking. Not once did she say how she would increase productivity.
I think the leader of the New Democratic Party insulted our intelligence yesterday in the example he put before us. He pointed out that if it cost $2 to produce one little gimmick and we were able to reduce the cost of production, the cost to the consumer would be that much less. This is elementary. We all agree that prosperity in this country is tied to our ability to increase productivity. This is the message all the way through the third annual review of the Economic Council of Canada. This is the message we got the other day from the gentleman from Sweden. This is the message we have had from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). This is the message of
November 22, 1966

Increased Cost of Living every economist in the country. We must increase productivity; we all agree with that. We are waiting for suggestions from the New Democratic Party on how to do it.
I remember the longshoremen's strike in the spring because I had an opportunity to pay close attention to it. Hon. members opposite are fond of rising and referring to the Pearson formula. Those hon. members are denying an economic fact about which we have just finished talking, namely, that increased salaries could be offset by increased productivity. We cannot castigate labour because they want their share of the profits. They are entitled to it for they are the ones who generate profits in this country. They should also play a role in increasing productivity, which was one of the opportunities offered to the longshoremen of Montreal.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
One of the things that disappointed me about the unions representing the longshoremen-I am sure tomorrow one of my friends in the New Democratic Party will acquaint them of my words-was their reluctance, at a time when they held their hands out for increased wages, to accept more sophisticated methods designed to increase productivity on the waterfront. You cannot have your cake and eat it too. They have to stop fearing technological change. They are espousing the same doctrine we used to hear from labour during the industrial revolution.

speechtext: Would the hon. member tell the house and the more than 6,000 automobile workers who have been laid off as a result of the U.S.-Canada auto pact what is the answer for them during this long period of lay-off?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
The answer does not lie in members of parliament, particularly those who represent the labour party, running up and down the country crying gloom and doom. This afternoon the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) spoke about productivity. He asked why we do not enjoy the same productivity as the United States. The answer is the size of markets. We all know it. I remember learning this lesson not too many years ago when I was in the manufacturing business producing sporting goods items. I went to a personal friend of mine in Brooklyn, of all places, who was manufacturing a particular item, which I wanted to manufacture, at a cost which seemed ridiculously low. It was so low that I could import it to Montreal and even after paying duties, tariffs and everything else, sell

it for a lot less than the cost of its manufacture here.
We searched for the reason and the reason was simple. That particular factory in Brooklyn sold more of that product on the island of Manhattan than there were potential customers in all of Canada. This is one of the reasons why we are at a disadvantage when we compare ourselves with American workers. This is one of the fundamental philosophies behind the automotive pact, that for the first time factories, particularly those producing auto parts in Canada, can have the benefit of extended runs because under the automotive pact they are able to supply auto factories in the United States on a competitive basis. This type of forward-looking and enlightened legislation is bound to have a disruptive effect on the labour market of Canada. It is unfortunate that it has turned out that one man's meat is another man's poison, but we are helping those who have been laid off.
Another by-product of the automotive pact is that it has spotlighted the fact that too many of our small secondary industries are inefficient and have fallen by the wayside. Those that had something to sell, were established and could compete once given a bigger market have flourished beyond the greatest expectations. While there may be lay-offs in some areas, there is tremendous employment in others, for instance, in the Windsor area where an acute housing situation was brought about by the hundreds and thousands of workers who flocked to that area because of the benefits of the automotive pact.
The very fact that the hon. member asked the question shows the isolationist and inward-looking type of thinking of his party. Certainly you cannot expect him to approve of the auto pact when every second speech we hear from them in the House of Commons from that party is anti-American. The only thing we do not hear from the New Democratic Party is that they are opposed to international unions because they do not dare say it. However, corporations are no good if their head offices are not in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have the time to offer the criticism which I would like to make of the remarks of the hon. member for Verdun but apparently he and his party are so divided in their policies that they can do nothing else but criticize other parties. It was most interesting to hear him, bankrupt of policies, frequently refer to the sound policies of the Conservative party which of course are lacking over there. As a matter of personal conviction and principle I feel compelled to place a certain matter before the house at this time. It will be recalled that on November 18 I
Increased Cost of Living asked a question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in the house in the following terms:
Mr. Speaker, will the new bonus to be paid bilingual civil servants also be paid to civil servants who are bilingual in any language combination other than English and French?
The Prime Minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I think the regulations in that regard are quite clear. I believe the bilingual bonus applies only to those having knowledge of the two official languages of Canada. If my friend the Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board could add anything to that, perhaps he would do so now.
The Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board said he would send me the regulation. In the meantime I had the opportunity of speaking to the Minister of National Revenue before he sent me the news release governing this policy. I asked him not to grant any bonuses or pay differentials along the narrow line adopted without including all those secretaries, stenographers and typists in the courts and in the federal service who, because of their position and location in the country, may be bilingual in other languages besides French or English.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION

Order, please. I wonder
whether the hon. member is suggesting to the house that the matter he is seeking to discuss relates to the amendment now before the house. As he knows we are only allowed to consider one grievance at a time and there is already one enshrined in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. The debate should be limited to that point as much as possible.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. My grievance is certainly in order at this time because it refers to salaries. It refers to the equitable distribution of the national income, as mentioned in the amendment. I remind the house that many questions arise from this latest policy of the government of giving a 7 per cent bonus to certain civil servants. What about the government clerk in Vancouver who may have to handle business between Japanese speaking, Chinese speaking or Hindustani speaking people and Her Majesty? If this clerk can speak any of these languages, and some people in British Columbia cannot fluently speak English, is he not entitled to this bonus?
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
What about the federal civil servant in the far north who has direct dealings with the Eskimos on behalf of Her Majesty and who

November 22, 1966
Division
speaks Eskimo as well as either French or English? What about federal civil servants in the prairie towns of the west who can and do speak Ukrainian, Polish, Hungarian, Russian or any of those other noble languages which are spoken by Canadians in these various localities? When a government clerk uses any of these languages to facilitate the necessary contacts between the government and these people, does he or she receive the 7 per cent bonus, a bonus which they deserve just as much as these more fortunate people referred to in this Liberal government news release?
What about the civil servant in Toronto dealing on behalf of the government with many thousands of Italian Canadians, many of whom cannot yet speak English or speak it well enough to converse fluently in a government office? If the government clerk or secretary can speak Italian as well as English and/or French, is not he of she just as deserving of this 7 per cent bonus as the more fortunate ones who have been given preference in this Liberal government news release?
The people of Canada are starting to ask questions, Mr. Speaker. They are dubious of the motives behind this Liberal measure by which the Prime Minister and his administration patronize and select a few at the expense of the rest of the people. This is nothing but discrimination almost bordering on something criminal in nature. This is typical of Liberal policy and it is nothing but a vote-getting stunt. It is nothing but an application of the nefarious Liberal characteristic of divide and conquer. This narrow, ill-conceived measure expounded in this news release of November 10 is discrimination at its worst. Under this measure we will have nothing but more trouble and discontent.
