speechtext:
Now that we have the promise from the minister that the next estimates to come before the house will go to a committee, we know we will have the opportunity to examine them more thoroughly. The minister tells us that the money has practically all been spent, so we will not quibble about that either. There are a few items about which I think the minister must inform the house. These concern projects which were to be cancelled because they were of an inflationary nature. At least they were not to be proceeded with this year. I think the minister should tell us which projects have been cancelled and which originally were cancelled and later proceeded with.
Everything is not wrong in the Department of Public Works. I can assure the minister of this. A first look at the blue book tells us that there has been a net decrease of 109 positions in all the votes in this department. I hope this has been as a result of efficiency and not as a result of there having been fewer projects across the country.
We all are happy with the increase in the grant to the Canadian Better Roads Association from $2,000 to $14,000. I would ask the minister in preparing the next estimates to consider making available a larger amount to this association so that in conjunction with research branches of the government it will be able to proceed further with research not only in respect of aggregates and other materials used on highways but also in respect of the problems involved in connection with drainage. Then there is the matter of the excessive damage done to the bodies of automobiles because of the erosion caused by the calcium and other chemical products. The expense which results from this erosion is serious, especially to the person who needs his car and considers it as a necessity because he loses much of the value of the automobile when he trades it in. There should definitely be more research along this line so that we may be able to eliminate this erosion.
I think the minister should explain to us how the amounts in the contingency fund are allotted. He should tell us how long this has

been included in the estimates and what purpose it serves in respect of salary increases. I know the minister is a busy man and he does not leave Ottawa very often, but I am wondering whether he should perhaps leave his office more frequently. I am sorry that during the past summer he did not make the trip to the lower St. Lawrence with the Postmaster General that he had planned, because I had a program outlined for him. I was going to take him to every harbour and wharf in the area. I had planned to show him what our problems are in that area. I am sure there are similar problems across the country. I would advise him to take some time off from his office duties occasionally so he can get out into the country to see how people are getting along. I think he would learn much more by visiting the areas in which the money administered by his department is being spent. Perhaps in this way he would be in a position to realize that possibly our requests of him are sometimes very sincere and very pressing.
The minister has varied interests to supervise. I should like to ask him, however, whether he contemplates closing down regional offices across the country, following the lead of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Department of Fisheries. I hope the minister is aware that these moves by the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Department of Fisheries have been criticized severely because they are putting people in a very disadvantageous position in these localities. Only last evening I was approached by one person who asked me whether it is true that a certain unemployment insurance office was being closed down. I said "yes". He said, "How am I going to be able to get my benefit cheques on time when I have to mail in my application and wait approximately a week or ten days?" This presents a problem because, as the minister must realize, when Canadians have to wait a week or so for a pay cheque in many cases their budgets are very seriously affected.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
There is a rumour abroad that the department intends to close down the regional office at Rimouski. I should like to speak for a few moments on this subject. There are approximately 200 establishments which the Department of Public Works looks after in this area. They are now going to move the regional office 200 miles away from the bulk of the activities in the area. This will make it rather difficult for the fishermen and commercial establishments in the area to get in touch
November 22, 1966

with the local engineers. If we are to double the number of engineers in the field, we are not being very efficient. Such a move must be considered a waste of money.
I have said before in the house that we are putting the administration on wheels. We will have no office close to the activities of the fishermen and the commercial establishments, and very often these facilities are needed by the fishermen. It will be impossible for these departmental people to be reached unless the fishermen or other business people are lucky enough to have them in the immediate area. I ask the government to reconsider this move, because if proceeded with it will adversely affect the fishermen of my area and, I am sure, those of many other areas.
The fishermen encounter many difficulties. They encounter difficulties with equipment which needs immediate repair, and so on. I would ask the minister whether the district engineers have sufficient authority to deal with these matters or are they limited in such a way that their efforts are ineffective? I know that in some cases we seem more concerned about being penny wise and pound foolish, but I know of cases where the taxi fares of employees are paid but the department will not pay the parking meter charges of its employees who use parking facilities for their cars in the exercise of their duties. This complaint may seem trivial but the employee is hindered in carrying out a really effective job.
My main concern about the administration of this department is its lack of co-ordination with other departments of government. I am not so concerned about the co-ordination of efforts in Ottawa but those in the field. There does not seem to be any integration of policies. Has the time not come when we should have regional co-ordinators? Only today I was reading the third annual review of the Economic Council of Canada, which recommends that there be co-ordination of all departments to see that there is no duplication of effort or loss or waste of money. Projects which we believe are important for an area are discarded or sent into limbo for years, while other projects which could wait for execution or realization are proceeded with.
Some research has to be carried out in this area. Projects should not proceed by guesswork. A little later I will deal with some of the plans drawn up by the Department of Public Works. Economic developments must be watched closely and the government's alertness must be evident. It must step in, if
Supply-Public Works
necessary, so that the impetus of a project will not be hindered or slowed down. Co-ordination in the different regions across the country would definitely be effective in ensuring that no time or effort is lost.
I can give the minister many examples of loss of time or effort in projects. If a federal regional co-ordinator had been present in these cases we could have avoided wasting money and priority jobs would have taken their rightful place. I can give the example of a public building where approximately 4,000 feet of floor space is not being utilized at the moment but only recently floor space was rented in an adjoining building to house federal employees. I am sure that if there had been co-ordination between the two departments of government this situation would not have occurred. There was a waste of money in this case.
I can also think of projects which have been proceeded with and given priority and on which we have spent as much as $4 million or $5 million, and on occasion only after the project was practically completed did we hire engineers to make a feasibility study. This in itself is quite all right if other projects do not suffer.
I can think of cases where producers have asked for the extension of a wharf. These are people who are shipping overseas to foreign markets. They have had to pay an additional $2, $3 or $4 per thousand feet to store their product some miles away from their establishments. If the minister, his department and the government would look closely into some of these projects they would find that such an investment by the government would encourage the producers and make it possible for them to realize a profit. It would make them competitive and enable them to remain in the market.
The employment of 1,000 people in one industry in one area is a matter of major importance. Therefore we should take a close, second look at these matters and give priority to the construction of wharves in the areas in which they are needed. I have written to the minister two or three times about such a project. I regret to say that his decision so far has not met with my approval or caused me any happiness.
Research must be undertaken in these fields. There must be co-ordination among departments. There must be co-ordination in the field among employees of different departments of government. I am certain that if we had this co-ordination we would attain a more

November 22, 1966
Supply-Public Works
efficient operation and provide a better service to the public. I am sure the minister wishes to see the greatest amount of efficiency in his department and is conscious of the welfare of the fishermen and the commercial operators. The minister, I am sure, wants his staff to be aware of local problems whether of supply or accommodation.
I hope that my suggestion with regard to regional co-ordinators will be taken seriously. Only last week in this house I raised a problem which concerned the Department of Transport and the Post Office Department. I am sure that if there had been co-ordination in the field between these two departments we could have encouraged an improvement in the transportation service in the area and provided a better mail service. This is the sort of problem which a local co-ordinator who knows the problems could deal with, and I suggest to the minister that if we had had a co-ordinator, one who would work in close co-operation with the Department of Fisheries-I am now speaking of problems with which I am familiar-we could have given a more efficient and practical service to that area.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Recently I spoke about my regret at the lack of co-ordination between employees of departments and I feel that co-ordination is lacking between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Fisheries. The employees of the Department of Fisheries know what is required in order that fishermen can better pursue their trade. This may be a small item to discuss but let us look at the effects which a $1,000 installation can have on fishermen in an area where they use the haul-up system. The sprocket, the chain or other parts of the equipment may break, but before we can get authorization to have it repaired a period of one week or ten days may elapse. During this time the fishermen cannot pursue their trade and it is easy to understand that they cannot afford to lose money or to lose one day of fishing.
This is just a small example to show what greater co-ordination between the different departments could do. The same thing applies to dredging operations across the country, for which a priority list is made up every year. Very often the judgment of the Department of Public Works does not quite coincide with that of the Department of Fisheries. Sometimes fishermen are forced to go from one area to another to pursue their trade and because of this they are not able to operate

efficiently. The same co-ordination should exist between the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works with regard to the lighting system which is required on public wharves and the directional lights needed by fishermen. I hope the minister will take these comments into consideration and will give thought to the appointment of a co-ordinator between his department, the Department of Fisheries, and other departments.
I should also like to know the policy of the Department of Public Works concerning protection walls. I believe that when erosion is caused by a public structure the department feel obliged to build a protection wall, but I do not understand their guidelines or criteria in determining whether a public structure has or has not caused erosion. What is the limiting line at which the engineer can determine that erosion is caused by a public structure up to line X and not line Y? I should like the minister to tell the house how this is determined.
I do not wish to criticize the engineers but I also find it difficult to understand the plan they use for hauling systems. In most of the areas I have visited I find that haul-ups are constructed in such a way that it is only at high tide and very often in a storm that a boat can approach these haul-ups directly. When a boat approaches a haul-up, how can one determine the ways and means of lifting it two or three feet out of the water to get it up on the haul? I am sorry that the minister did not make his projected trip last summer because I would have shown him some of the designs that are being used. Although he is not an engineer I am sure he is practical enough to realize that it is time we changed the design.
I hope the minister does not think I have criticized him but rather that I have brought up some of the problems which exist all across the country where public works are concerned, and as the appropriate items come before the house I will have more detailed questions to ask of the minister.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot resist making a few brief remarks because I have had a long association with the Department of Public Works which has extended over 55 years. I have taken part in building bridges inspecting wharves and inspecting timbers and lumber used in small wharves. Possibly I feel more at home in this field than in some other quarters.
I was pleased to hear the minister mention that next session these estimates will be sent
November 22, 1966

to a committee. I think this is a very good idea because many members are interested in getting to know more about the operation of this department in Ottawa and in the various regional offices and districts. In committee they will be able to inquire into the various functions which the department performs at the present time and which have been greatly enlarged in recent years.
There is one matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention. The residents in my riding along the Columbia River are interested in the arrangements that are being made between the federal Department of Public Works and the British Columbia hydro authority or the British Columbia government, whichever is responsible, for the relocation of wharves until the time when the dam is completed. They would also like to know what is being done with respect to the rebuilding of certain riprap mattresses which are required to prevent erosion of the very steep sandy banks along sharp curves in the river which have to be protected if navigation is to proceed normally. The chamber of commerce in that area and the farmers' institute as well as other organizations are interested in these matters which are under the jurisdiction of this department.
I understand that the Department of Public Works has decided on the location of a wharf at one point for launches, tugs and so on. This has caused other communities to wonder what will be done in their areas. I would very much like to know about this, and if it is not possible for the minister to give details on it tonight possibly he could send me a few lines.
The next matter deals with the question of casual employees. All the men working on the repairing of wharves are experienced and many of them are getting on in years. I do hope that everything possible is being done to give these people as much employment as is possible. You need skilled men to build a wharf, run a pile driver or operate a dredge and you will not get these men unless you provide work for them between seasons even if you have to transfer them from one lake to another or from one interior district to another. I hope that everything will be done to maintain a corps of experienced men for the operation of a dredge, the running of a pile driver and the building of wharves and riprap mattresses which we know will be required in a year or two from now.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Another matter I wish to mention is the question of the pension fund, about which I 23033-647
Supply-Public Works
have had some correspondence. I understand that there are some of these casual employees who are out of employment for four or five months in the year but who are paying up to $30 a month into the civil service pension fund. This is another reason that everything possible should be done to give these persons as much employment as possible. As I said before, many of them are on in years and their families are resident in the district, but if necessary they could go to other points for a month or two to maintain their employment. I bring this matter to the minister's attention and I am sure that his senior officials know of the circumstances.
I am interested in the item dealing with testing laboratories, and next year when the estimates go before a committee I hope that those responsible for the operation of these laboratories will have the opportunity to explain to the members of the committee what work is being undertaken at this time. I suppose it is related to steel, concrete and the various materials used in the construction of buildings and wharves as well as other projects undertaken by this department.
Once again, Mr. Chairman, I refer to the question of the design of buildings. I think that the Department of Public Works could use a little more imagination than they have to date in the design of buildings, especially in smaller communities, in order that they will fit in, shall I say, with the locality in which they are erected. We have standard-size post offices throughout the country and standard-size R.C.M.P. buildings and other buildings of this type. I think something can be done to use a little more imagination to make these buildings more suitable to the locality in which they are erected so that they become a more worthy addition to the community, more artistic and satisfactory from the aesthetic point of view.
In view of the work which will have to be done on the Arrow Lakes and portions of the Kootenay Lakes owing to the building of the Columbia River treaty projects and because of the need for wharves to be replaced, I hope that the district office in Nelson will be kept open. The men on the job know more about the immediate work to be done than people here in Ottawa because they know the local circumstances and conditions in which they work. They know about the materials and so on. So I hope the district office will not be closed.
Another growing requirement in this district is the need for more launching ramps for

November 22, 1966
Supply-Public Works
the launching of boats by tourists. Last year over 150 boats came up from Portland via the Columbia River to the Arrow Lakes and many points as far north as Revelstoke. This traffic is increasing and provision is being made for these boats. In some cases they are taken around dams in the United States such as Grand Coulee, Boulder and so on by lowboys and in Canada they go through locks. This traffic is increasing and will increase even more in the years ahead.
In addition, large numbers of pleasure launches are being towed into the area by automobiles and there is a great need for launching ramps. I am not suggesting that this is something which is required immediately, but I would suggest that the engineers in the department should survey the district and in small communities which make the best part of their income from the tourist industry consideration should be given to erecting launching ramps at suitable points near the communities.
I think that is all I wish to raise at the present time, Mr. Chairman. I want to compliment the officials in Ottawa and the district officials in British Columbia, as well as the local officials and employees who work in my constituency. As I have said before, I have always had a close association with this department. I have known most of the local men for a great number of years and the work they do, and when I make a request on their behalf I am actually speaking for them.

speechtext:
There is just one point I want to discuss, Mr. Chairman, on the estimates of the Minister of Public Works, I refer the contribution made to the provinces under the provisions of the Trans-Canada Highway Act.
This matter has been talked about a number of times in this house. I notice there is an item of $52,600,000 for this fiscal year. The injustice of the present payment is that the provinces that went ahead and complied with the terms of the original Trans-Canada Highway Act are actually being penalized for having done so because the percentage of contribution has been changed two or three times since the original act was passed. I think that now the federal government is paying as much as 90 per cent of the cost. Furthermore, this very high percentage of cost applies to the most expensive section of the road passing through the provinces. One thing we object to is that payment is not made retroactive for those provinces which finished the highway long ago but now have to modernize it.

I am sure the Minister of Public Works will agree that when the house passed the original Trans-Canada Highway Act in the early 1950's the intent of the act was that there would at least be one modern highway across Canada from one end to the other. In many areas, particularly in Alberta and Saskatchewan, two provinces which finished their sections first, the highway is now ten years or a little more old and is not up to the specifications required today for a modern highway. One section I particularly refer to is from Calgary to Banff national park. When this section was built the specifications called for a certain width of highway, for certain compaction and so on, sufficient at the time for the amount of traffic using the highway. However, today the department of highways has found from surveys that there is a requirement for a four-lane highway and this is being built. Traffic counts have been made and today's requirements call for certain underpasses and overpasses which add substantially to the cost.
All I am saying to the minister is that the government ought to take another look at the legislation and its intent, because I am sure he will agree that this house directed the government to construct at least one modern highway from one end of the country to the other. But the specifications laid down in the early 1950's are no longer adequate for modern highway requirements. I hope that before the minister's estimates come before the house next session he will take into account the fact that the federal parliament has indicated that it wants the federal treasury to become involved in this kind of undertaking, whether to the extent of 50 per cent or some other figure, on a continuing basis so as to keep this highway up to modern-day requirements.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
If a highway falls behind the times it becomes obsolete. I suggest to the minister that after ten years it is not unreasonable to say that in many areas this highway is old fashioned. Therefore the federal government should not withdraw from this project and leave the provinces to do all the maintenance and modernization. In some sections of Alberta the modernization that has gone on in the last two or three years has cost far more in dollars per mile than the original construction cost of the highway. I hope the minister will take this into account. I raised this question last year and had a sympathetic response. So far nothing has happened. I hope the minister will give consideration to what I have said.
November 22, 1966

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
It would be useful if I took a moment to clear up one or two points which have been raised. I will not attempt to deal with all but there are one or two items which I think should be clarified right away.
The hon. member for Gaspe spoke about the desirability of trips to different parts of the country and I think he had in mind the Gaspe region. If he had, I have no criticism of him for that because I had such a trip planned last fall. Unfortunately the railway strike occurred necessitating the sitting of parliament and the trip was cancelled. I assure the hon. member that I want to visit outlying areas of the country, particularly the Gaspe area, and particularly do I want to look at that large project under way at Matane. There are many other projects along the whole coast that I want to look at. There is one point I should clear up so that there will be no uncertainty about it. It has to do with the Rimouski district office. That office will be continued. There is no suggestion of closing it at the moment. I thought I should put that on the record.
As to the public building with 4,000 square feet of space not used, I would be grateful to the hon. member if he would let me have the details so that the matter can be looked into immediately.
With regard to protection works, that has always been a very difficult problem, as the hon. member indicated. I would be glad to set out in as precise a way as I can the criteria we seek to apply, though I am fully cognizant of the difficulties of making a determination whether damage is due to erosion, to natural forces, to navigation or to the erection of some structure by the federal government.
The hon. member for Kootenay West raised some questions and I will try to answer one or two of them. He made particular reference to the relocation of wharves because of the rising of the water by reason of the construction of the High Arrow dam. The arrangement is that the responsibility for paying for this will be that of B.C. Hydro but the work will be done in conjunction with the Department of Public Works, because some new wharves may not be in close proximity to others that are being flooded out. As the hon. member will agree, there may be some relocations necessary of a substantial sort and that can be done in conjunction with the Department of Public Works. But the actual liability, if you want to call it that, for reconstruction because of this dam is that of B.C. Hydro. The methods of protection against erosion are to be
23033-647a
Supply-Public Works
treated the same way. Perhaps I should extend my remarks on erosion to indicate that the federal responsibility in this field is only where erosion is due to navigation or to the erection of public works.
The hon. member made some extended remarks about personnel matters and I would prefer, rather than giving an off-hand answer, to look at the points he raised in a specific way to see what can be done to better the conditions of the employees who have less than full-time employment. I shall also look at the related matters he raised having to do with pension contributions.
The hon. member also made reference to the district office in Nelson. My understanding is that it is not a district office as such but that it is an arrangement whereby we keep one man posted at Nelson. I do not want to go on record that we are maintaining a district office at Nelson because that is not what we call it in the department and it might be misleading to call it that.

On the question of launching ramps the situation there is that the policy as announced in August last year has aroused tremendous interest in the country and the demands for assistance in this area are coming in at a pace really precluding a reasonable prospect of adequate servicing at the moment. It is a policy we are trying to develop. We are trying to examine each application to see how it meets the criteria laid down at that time. We are doing the preliminary studies so that a priority for this policy can be established that would have a reasonable expectation of being carried out.

No, Mr. Chairman, I would not agree with that suggestion. The intent of the original act was that the federal government would contribute to the construction of this highway. In view of the fact that it is under provincial jurisdiction, it was intended that a highway be constructed across this country up to the modern standards which prevailed at that time. The Grand river from early times, from the opening of settlement in this country, has been one of the greatest water thoroughfares in Canada. This is particularly true since the advent of the railway.
Today the country is becoming more heavily populated, particularly in this area of Ontario, and the need for recreational facilities is becoming greater each week. No better area could be found for recreational purposes than the beautiful Grand river valley. Many members of parliament on both sides of this house come from that area and I know they will back me in my request to the minister who is, as I said a moment ago, a very imaginative man.
Let me remind the minister that this river has in recent years been badly polluted but that the situation has been corrected as a result of the foresight of provincial authorities. These authorities have forced municipalities and commercial enterprises along the river to stop dumping sewage into it. Sewage disposal plants have been constructed in every major municipality along the Grand river. I cannot think of a more wonderful place for boating. It would be a Godsend to our area and sooner or later this will take place if this area is redeveloped for recreational purposes. I can guarantee to the house that following redevelopment, this area will form the largest single recreational area on the North American continent. It begins behind the city of Hamilton and continues along the historic waterway past the Six Nations Indian reservation where the flag of England was planted. This is an area where loyalty to the Crown is one of the most important characteristics of the population.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may seem a little like dealing with an inconsequential matter after the disgraceful statement tonight by the Minister of Labour, but I am in the position of having to address myself to the subject matter set down for debate.
I may say first of all that on November 18 I discovered that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) is a much maligned individual in this house. He has been variously classified as a verbalist whose loquacity is only exceeded by the scarcity of information which is contained in his verbose statements. However, this was proven the other day to be a base canard of the worst sort because I asked him a question on Friday, November 18, reported at page 10048 of Hansard as follows:
I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and ask him whether during his visit to the Soviet Union he discussed with officials there the prospects of the U.S.S.R. at least entering into talks about the entry of that nation into the North Pacific Fisheries Treaty pact?
To which the Secretary of State for External Affairs replied with a succinct "No, Mr. Speaker". I was so taken aback by the sharpness of that reply that I missed the opportunity to ask him a supplementary question. The fact is that his reply indicates that the government has absolutely no interest whatever in entering into discussions with a major fishing nation about the conservation and preservation of fishery stocks in the north Pacific ocean. Since 1953, Japan, United States and Canada have been signatories to a treaty to conserve the stocks of salmon, halibut and herring in the north Pacific ocean. The Soviet Union is a prime fishing nation of these species of fish, and as we all know its fishing fleet has ranged close to and perhaps within our 12 mile-limit off the coast of British Columbia.
Prior to the election the government now in office ranged across the country and, coming close to my community on the Pacific coast, promised that it was dedicated to bringing the Soviet union into the North Pacific fisheries pact. The Secretary of State for External Affairs had the opportunity to raise the matter when he went to the Soviet union with the heads of that state to see if they were interested in coming into the NORPAC treaty. He said that he did not even discuss the matter,
10230	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion that he completely ignored it. That is an absolute disgrace, and it should be an eye-opener to the fishermen on the Pacific coast it they listen to the bull about the desire of the Liberal party to take worth-while steps to conserve the fisheries stock off the Pacific coast.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs undoubtedly has valid reasons for not being here this evening to comment but I notice that the Minister of Fisheries is here. Perhaps that minister will now take this opportunity to give some worthwhile information to the house about what has been done to entice the Soviet Union into the North Pacific fisheries treaty. So far any information the government may have at its disposal has been kept secret. We want to know what it is, and certainly the fishermen of British Columbia want to know.

I believe our worries in this regard are well founded. As yet I have not been convinced that these speeds have been set because of a security reason. The people in this area are of the belief that C.N.R. officials are developing an argument against our request to have the Chaleur travel directly between Montreal and Gaspe. It is our belief that the C.N.R. will propose the argument that because the 30 mile an hour speed limit was ordered on October 30, 1966, our request cannot be met. This is of great concern to the people in this area.
I have been asked to bring this question to the attention of the minister and it is my
November 22, 1966	COMMONS
hope, as well as the hope of those whom 1 represent, that I am wrong in both my suggestions as to the reasons for these speed limits. We hope that our request for improved passenger service will be met and that the Cha-leur will travel directly from Montreal to Gaspe.
